57.title: Who do you say I am? (Matthew 16:13–20)
57.hook: Peter answers first, and is given a name meaning rock and the keys of the kingdom
57.howItsDone: Catholics keep the Chair of Saint Peter on February 22, and churches East and West keep Saints Peter and Paul on June 29. Many Christians describe coming to faith as answering this question for themselves, and some churches ask it in confirmation or at baptism.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter walks on water: he stepped out, sank as a man of oligopistos, and was caught. Your line was he catches the sinking. What step did you take? Today a new stretch begins: Jerusalem and the last week. Day fifty-seven.

People ask what you do for work, where you're from, what you're into. It's rare that someone asks who you think they are. Matthew sets this scene in the far north, in the region of Caesarea Philippi, a town whose very name honored Caesar. Jesus and his disciples are walking, and he asks them an easy question first: what are people saying about me? Then a hard one. Today's word: the keys.
screen: `WHO DO YOU THINK THEY ARE?` → `CAESAREA PHILIPPI, FAR NORTH.` → `AN EASY QUESTION, THEN A HARD ONE.`

segments.voice: The easy question, in the King James Bible: "Whom do men say that I the Son of man am?" The answers come quickly. Some say John the Baptist, back from the dead. Some say Elijah. Others, Jeremiah, or one of the prophets. Then he turns it: "But whom say ye that I am?" You. Not the crowds. And Peter answers: "Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God." Christ is the Greek for the Hebrew Messiah: the anointed one, the king God promised. Jesus calls him blessed, and says this didn't come from any human being, but from his Father in heaven. Then he gives Simon a new name: "thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it." There's a pun inside. In Greek, Peter is Petros, and rock is petra. And John's Gospel gives Peter's name in Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke, as Cephas, which it says means a stone; Paul calls him Cephas too. Some readers hear one Aramaic word, kepha, under both halves of the line. Then: "And I will give unto thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven." Keys meant authority, the steward of a house who opens and shuts the doors. Here Christians read differently, and deeply. Catholics understand the rock as Peter himself, with his authority passed on to the bishops of Rome; the keys appear on the papal coat of arms. Orthodox Christians honor Peter as first among the apostles, and many of their teachers read the rock as Peter's confession of faith, with authority held by the bishops together. Many Protestants read the rock as that confession, or as Christ himself. The question itself reads the same in every Bible: who do you say I am?
screen: `WHOM DO MEN SAY THAT I AM?` · `BUT WHOM SAY YE?` · `PETROS, PETRA, CEPHAS.` · `THE KEYS: WHO OPENS AND SHUTS.` · then, large: `THOU ART THE CHRIST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit comfortably, and let your breathing slow. Now let the question come to you, just as it came to them. Not what your parents said. Not what your church says, or your friends, or the internet. Who do you say he is? A teacher. A prophet. The Christ. A question mark. Someone you're still meeting. There's no wrong answer in the privacy of your own head, and nobody's grading it. Just be honest with yourself. If you pray, you can bring your answer to God as it is. The bell holds the time.
The keys. The authority to open and shut, given to Peter, the rock, after he answered the hard question. Churches read the keys in different ways.
Your line: the question is for you. Today, when someone asks what you think, pause and give your own answer, not the crowd's. Day fifty-seven.

58.title: The mountain of light (Matthew 17:1–8)
58.hook: on a mountain his face shines like the sun, and Peter wants to build tents
58.carry: you can't stay on the mountain
58.howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches keep the feast of the Transfiguration on August 6, and many Protestant churches read the story on the Sunday before Lent. On that day many Orthodox churches bless the first fruits of the harvest, often grapes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the keys, and a hard question: who do you say I am? Your line was the question is for you. What did you answer? Six days later, Matthew says, they climb a mountain. Day fifty-eight.

A sunrise that stops the car. A newborn's first cry. The last chord of a song, before anyone claps. Some moments seem lit from the inside, and nobody wants them to end. Matthew says Jesus takes just three of his friends, Peter, James and John, up a high mountain, away from everyone. Matthew doesn't name the mountain. Tradition says it was Mount Tabor, in Galilee, a round hill rising alone from the plain. And up there, in front of them, something happens. Today's word: transfiguration.
screen: `A MOMENT LIT FROM INSIDE.` → `THREE FRIENDS, A HIGH MOUNTAIN.` → `SOMETHING HAPPENS.`

segments.voice: Matthew says he was transfigured before them, in the King James Bible: "and his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light." The Greek word is metamorphoo, the root of our metamorphosis: changed in form. The Latin became transfiguration. And then two more figures appear, talking with him: Moses, who gave the law, and Elijah, the great prophet. Some readers see the law and the prophets standing together on one mountain. Then Peter, who never seems to stay quiet for long, says something practical: "Lord, it is good for us to be here: if thou wilt, let us make here three tabernacles; one for thee, and one for Moses, and one for Elias." Tabernacles means tents, shelters. Let's build something. Let's stay. While he's still talking, a bright cloud covers them, and a voice says what it said at the river: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him." Hear him. Not build for him. The disciples fall on their faces, terrified. And then the gentlest moment. Jesus comes and touches them: "Arise, and be not afraid." They look up, and there's no one but Jesus. Then they walk back down the mountain, and waiting at the bottom is a crowd, and a father with a sick boy. The light doesn't last. Life resumes. Orthodox Christians give this story a special place, and speak of the light on the mountain as God's own light, which the saints can come to share. Many churches keep the feast on August sixth.
screen: `METAMORPHOSIS: CHANGED IN FORM.` · `MOSES AND ELIJAH APPEAR.` · `LET US MAKE THREE TENTS.` · `BACK DOWN TO THE CROWD.` · then, large: `HIS FACE DID SHINE AS THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and close your eyes if you like. Go looking for one moment of pure light in your own life. It doesn't have to be religious. A morning, a face, a song, a place, a silence. Bring it back as clearly as you can: the light, the sound, the air. Stay with it for a few breaths. Then, gently, let it go, and notice that you're still carrying something of it. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. The bell holds the time.
Transfiguration. From the Latin, and behind it the Greek for metamorphosis: changed in form. On a mountain his face shone like the sun.
Your line: you can't stay on the mountain. Today, remember your moment of light, and then take some of it down to someone who needs it. Day fifty-eight.

59.title: Zacchaeus up a tree (Luke 19:1–10)
59.hook: a short, hated tax collector climbs a sycamore; Jesus invites himself for dinner
59.howItsDone: Many churches read the story of Zacchaeus at the dedication of a church building, and it's a favorite in children's Sunday school, often with a song. Christians often point to it when speaking of restitution: making amends in practical ways.

segments.voice: Yesterday, transfiguration: a face like the sun, and Peter wanting to build tents. Your line was you can't stay on the mountain. Who did you carry the light to? Now the road runs south, through Jericho. Day fifty-nine.

Remember being the short kid at a parade, or at the back of a concert, bouncing on your toes and seeing nothing but shoulders? This is Jericho, an old city on the road up to Jerusalem. Jesus is passing through, and the streets are packed. One man wants very badly to see him. His name is Zacchaeus. Luke says he's the chief among the publicans, the tax collectors, and he's rich. Before this story ends, the whole crowd will call him a sinner. Nobody's going to make room for him. And he's short. So a grown, wealthy, powerful, unpopular man runs ahead and does something undignified. Today, sycamore.
screen: `BOUNCING ON YOUR TOES.` → `A CROWD IN JERICHO.` → `A SHORT, RICH, HATED MAN.`

segments.voice: Luke says he "climbed up into a sycomore tree to see him: for he was to pass that way." A sycamore fig, a wide, low tree with branches easy to climb, not the American sycamore. There he is, a rich official, sitting in a tree like a boy. And Jesus reaches the spot, stops, looks up, and says his name: "Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house." Luke doesn't say how he knows the name. And he doesn't wait for an invitation. He invites himself to dinner. Zacchaeus scrambles down and welcomes him joyfully. But the crowd grumbles, all of them, Luke says: "That he was gone to be guest with a man that is a sinner." And then, before anyone asks him to, Zacchaeus stands up and says: "Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold." Fourfold. The law of Moses asked a thief to pay back four sheep for one stolen sheep. Zacchaeus holds himself to the thief's standard, on his own. Notice the order. Jesus didn't say, change first, then I'll come. He called him by name, came to his house, and the change came after, freely. Then Jesus says: "This day is salvation come to this house," and gives a line some readers take as a summary of Luke's whole Gospel: "For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost." And a small irony some readers hear in his name, which they link to a Hebrew word for pure. The whole town called him a sinner. Jesus called him by his name.
screen: `UP A SYCAMORE FIG.` · `ZACCHAEUS, MAKE HASTE, AND COME DOWN.` · `THE CROWD GRUMBLES.` · `HALF TO THE POOR, FOURFOLD BACK.` · then, large: `TO SEEK AND TO SAVE THAT WHICH WAS LOST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let your breathing slow. Think of one thing you got wrong with someone. Not the worst thing you ever did. Something you could actually fix. Money you owe. A promise you broke. Credit you took that wasn't yours. A harsh word you never took back. Picture the person. Now picture what making it right would look like. Maybe a message, a payment, an apology, a phone call. Don't beat yourself up. Zacchaeus didn't. He just stood up and said what he'd do. If you pray, you can ask for the courage. The bell holds the time.
Sycamore. A wide, low fig tree with branches easy to climb, the one a rich, short, unpopular tax collector climbed just to see Jesus pass by.
Your line: he knows your name. Today, make one thing right that you got wrong. Start small, but start. Day fifty-nine.

60.title: Lazarus, come out (John 11:1–44)
60.hook: Jesus weeps at his friend's tomb, then calls him out
60.howItsDone: Many churches read the raising of Lazarus near the end of Lent, and Orthodox Christians keep Lazarus Saturday the day before Palm Sunday. Jesus's words I am the resurrection, and the life are read at many Christian funerals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zacchaeus up a sycamore, called down by name. Your line was he knows your name. What did you make right? Today, a friend's name called into a tomb. Day sixty.

Think of the phone call nobody wants. Someone you love is sick, and you're far away, and you have to decide how fast to come. Now go to Bethany, a village just outside Jerusalem. Two sisters, Martha and Mary, send word to Jesus about their brother Lazarus. Their words, in the King James Bible, are simple: "Lord, behold, he whom thou lovest is sick." Not our brother. The one you love. They were close friends. And John says something puzzling: Jesus loved them, and so he stayed where he was two more days. By the time he arrives, Lazarus has been in the tomb four days. Today's word: Lazarus.
screen: `THE PHONE CALL NOBODY WANTS.` → `HE WHOM THOU LOVEST IS SICK.` → `FOUR DAYS IN THE TOMB.`

segments.voice: Martha hears he's coming and runs out to meet him on the road, and she's honest: if you had been here, my brother wouldn't have died. And he tells her: "I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live." Then Mary comes, and she falls at his feet and says the very same words: if you had been here. She's weeping, and everyone with her is weeping. And John says he was deeply moved and troubled. He asks, where have you laid him? They say, come and see. And then the shortest verse in the English Bible, two words: "Jesus wept." Think about that. He knows what he's about to do. He's about to call Lazarus out. And he still weeps. He doesn't skip past the grief to the happy ending. He stands in it with his friends. The people watching say: "Behold how he loved him!" At the tomb he says, take away the stone, and practical Martha objects, in the King James words: "Lord, by this time he stinketh: for he hath been dead four days." They roll it away anyway. He prays aloud, then shouts: "Lazarus, come forth." And the dead man walks out, still wrapped hand and foot in grave clothes, his face bound with a cloth. And the last line is almost tender in its plainness: "Loose him, and let him go." Somebody has to unwrap him. In John's Gospel this is the last and greatest sign before the cross, and it's the one that makes the authorities decide he must die. The name Lazarus comes from the Hebrew Eleazar: God has helped.
screen: `IF THOU HADST BEEN HERE.` · `I AM THE RESURRECTION.` · `TWO WORDS: JESUS WEPT.` · `LOOSE HIM, AND LET HIM GO.` · then, large: `LAZARUS, COME FORTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let your shoulders drop. Is there one thing you haven't let yourself cry about? A loss, a disappointment, a door that closed, a person who's gone. Something you moved past too quickly because there was too much to do. Let it come to mind. You don't have to force tears. Just stop holding it back. If tears come, let them. Jesus wept at a tomb he was about to open. Grief isn't a lack of faith. If you pray, you can bring the grief as it is. The bell holds the time.
Lazarus. From the Hebrew Eleazar, God has helped. A friend four days in the tomb, wept over, and called out by name.
Your line: jesus wept. Today, let yourself feel one grief instead of rushing past it, and if someone near you is grieving, don't hurry them either. Day sixty.

61.title: A king on a donkey (Luke 19:28–40)
61.hook: crowds wave branches and throw coats on the road for a man on a borrowed donkey
61.howItsDone: Many churches keep Palm Sunday, the start of Holy Week, with palm branches, a procession and readings of the entry into Jerusalem. In many churches the Sanctus, sung in the communion prayers, ends with Hosanna in the highest.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lazarus, called out of the tomb, and your line: jesus wept. What grief did you let yourself feel? Today, the last week begins, and the road goes up into Jerusalem. Day sixty-one.

Motorcades. Tinted windows. Security in dark suits. A red carpet. That's how power tends to arrive. This arrival starts on the road over the Mount of Olives toward Jerusalem, with the city filling up for Passover. Jesus sends two disciples ahead to a village with strange instructions: you'll find a colt tied up that no one has ever ridden. Untie it and bring it. If anyone asks why, say this: "The Lord hath need of him." They go, and it's exactly as he said. The owners ask, the disciples answer, and the owners let it go. A borrowed donkey. Today's word: hosanna.
screen: `MOTORCADES AND RED CARPETS.` → `A COLT NO ONE HAS RIDDEN.` → `THE LORD HATH NEED OF HIM.`

segments.voice: They throw their coats over the colt, and set Jesus on it. And as he rides, people spread their coats on the road in front of him, a red carpet made of whatever they're wearing. As he comes down the Mount of Olives, the whole crowd of his followers starts shouting, in Luke's words in the King James Bible: "Blessed be the King that cometh in the name of the Lord: peace in heaven, and glory in the highest." Now today's word. Luke doesn't use it, but Matthew, Mark and John do, and it's the word the crowd shouted, in Matthew: "Hosanna to the son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord; Hosanna in the highest." Hosanna comes from Hebrew, hoshia na, and it means save, please. It comes from Psalm 118, the psalm the crowd is quoting, where the King James Bible renders it: "Save now, I beseech thee, O LORD." Over time it became a shout of praise, but underneath it's a cry for help: save us, now. And John adds the palm branches, which is why churches call this Palm Sunday. Why a donkey? The prophet Zechariah had said Jerusalem's king would come "lowly, and riding upon an ass." And in the next verse the horse is cut off from Jerusalem, and the king speaks peace. This is a king arriving in a way no emperor would. Some of the Pharisees in the crowd tell him to quiet his followers. And he says: "I tell you that, if these should hold their peace, the stones would immediately cry out." Christians still shout hosanna in worship. Catholics, Orthodox, Anglicans, Lutherans and others sing it in the communion prayers, before the bread and cup are shared.
screen: `COATS ON THE ROAD.` · `HOSANNA: SAVE, PLEASE.` · `A DONKEY, NOT A WAR HORSE.` · `THE STONES WOULD CRY OUT.` · then, large: `BLESSED BE THE KING THAT COMETH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and breathe slowly. The crowd laid down their coats, the thing they had on them, so someone else's way would be smoother. Think of one person in your life whose road could use smoothing today. What could you lay down for them? Your turn to talk. Your preferred plan. Your seat. An hour of your time. Your need to be right. Picture yourself laying it down in front of them. If you pray, you can say the old word, hosanna: save, please. The bell holds the time.
Hosanna. From the Hebrew hoshia na: save, please. A cry for help that became a shout of praise, sung for a king on a donkey.
Your line: the stones would cry out. Today, lay something down for someone, quietly, the way they laid down their coats. Day sixty-one.

62.title: The tables go over (Matthew 21:12–13)
62.hook: in the temple courts he overturns the money changers' tables
62.howItsDone: Many churches read the cleansing of the temple in Lent or Holy Week. Christians often turn to it when thinking about keeping places of worship for prayer, and about money and faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hosanna: save, please, shouted for a king on a donkey. Your line was the stones would cry out. What did you lay down? Today the gentle king walks into the temple, and things get loud. Day sixty-two.

Children taken up in his arms. Hands on the sick. A king on a donkey. And then this scene. The temple in Jerusalem, days before Passover: the center of Jewish worship, and packed. Pilgrims have come from everywhere. The outer court, a huge open space, is full of stalls: people selling doves and animals for the sacrifices, and money changers at their tables. Noise, bargaining, animals, crowds. And Jesus walks in. Today, moneychangers.
screen: `CHILDREN, THE SICK, A DONKEY.` → `THE TEMPLE BEFORE PASSOVER.` → `STALLS, COINS AND DOVES.`

segments.voice: Matthew tells it fast, in the King James Bible: "And Jesus went into the temple of God, and cast out all them that sold and bought in the temple, and overthrew the tables of the moneychangers, and the seats of them that sold doves." Coins spilling across the stones. Birds flapping. Then he explains, quoting two prophets at once: "It is written, My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves." The first half is from Isaiah, and in Mark's telling the full line appears: a house of prayer for all nations. The second half is from Jeremiah, who stood in the gate of the temple of his own day and warned people not to treat God's house as a den, a hideout. So this isn't an attack on the temple, or on Judaism. It's a Jewish prophet in the line of Isaiah and Jeremiah, calling the temple back to what it was for. And the selling itself served a purpose: pilgrims who came from far away needed doves and animals to offer, and someone to change their money. But some readers point out that the stalls likely stood in the outer court, where people who weren't Jewish could come and pray. If that court is a market, where do they go? Make room for prayer. All four Gospels tell this story; John puts it near the start of Jesus's work, and adds a whip of cords. And look at what Matthew says happens right after the tables go over. The blind and the lame come to him in the temple, and he heals them. And children start shouting hosanna. The noise of trade gives way to the noise of healing and praise.
screen: `HE OVERTHREW THE TABLES.` · `A HOUSE OF PRAYER FOR ALL NATIONS.` · `A PROPHET LIKE JEREMIAH.` · `THEN THE BLIND AND THE LAME COME.` · then, large: `MY HOUSE SHALL BE CALLED THE HOUSE OF PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and look around the space you're in. Think of one cluttered corner in your life. It might be a real corner: a desk, a shelf, a car seat, a phone's home screen. Or a crowded hour of your day with no room left in it. Picture what that space would look like if it were clear, with room to breathe, room to think, room to pray if you pray. You don't have to clear it all right now. Just decide which one small table you'll turn over today. The bell holds the time.
Moneychangers. The traders Jesus found at their tables in the temple's outer court, and sent scattering so the court could be, again, a house of prayer.
Your line: make room for prayer. Today, clear one cluttered corner, and leave it empty for a while. Day sixty-two.

63.title: The jar of perfume (John 12:1–8)
63.hook: Mary of Bethany pours a year's wages of perfume on his feet
63.howItsDone: Many churches read the anointing at Bethany in Holy Week, and in Catholic and Orthodox churches, anointing with oil and perfume remains part of baptism, confirmation or chrismation, and prayer for the sick. Mary of Bethany is remembered with her sister Martha and brother Lazarus.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tables go over on the moneychangers, and a prophet's cry: my house shall be called the house of prayer. Your line was make room for prayer. What corner did you clear? Today ends week nine. Day sixty-three.

Flowers that cost too much. A friend who drives all night to be there. A gift so over the top that nobody at the party knows where to look. Back in Bethany, six days before Passover, John says, they make Jesus a supper. Lazarus, the friend called out of the tomb, is at the table. His sister Martha is serving. And their sister Mary brings out a pound of very costly ointment. Today, spikenard.
screen: `A GIFT THAT'S TOO MUCH.` → `SIX DAYS BEFORE PASSOVER.` → `MARY BRINGS THE OINTMENT.`

segments.voice: John tells it in one long breath, in the King James Bible: "Then took Mary a pound of ointment of spikenard, very costly, and anointed the feet of Jesus, and wiped his feet with her hair: and the house was filled with the odour of the ointment." Spikenard, or nard, was a precious perfumed oil, and John calls it very costly. And she doesn't dab it. She pours out a whole pound on his feet, and then she wipes them with her own hair, in front of everyone. And the whole house smells of it. You can't hide this kind of love. Then Judas speaks, and on paper he has a point: "Why was not this ointment sold for three hundred pence, and given to the poor?" Three hundred pence, three hundred denarii. In Matthew's parable of the vineyard, a laborer is paid a penny a day. So this is three hundred days of work. John adds, bluntly, that Judas kept the common purse and helped himself from it. Jesus answers: "Let her alone: against the day of my burying hath she kept this." Later in John, his body is wrapped with spices for the grave. Mary, it seems, understood something the others didn't: he was about to die. Then: "For the poor always ye have with you; but me ye have not always." That line has been misused to excuse ignoring the poor. But it echoes Deuteronomy, where the same thought comes with a command: open your hand wide to the poor. One way to hear it: the choice isn't generosity or love. Some moments come only once. This week began with Peter's answer and the keys. Then the mountain of light, Zacchaeus, Lazarus, hosanna, the tables. And now a jar poured out.
screen: `A POUND OF SPIKENARD.` · `SHE WIPED HIS FEET WITH HER HAIR.` · `A YEAR'S WAGES, SAYS JUDAS.` · `AGAINST THE DAY OF MY BURYING.` · then, large: `THE HOUSE WAS FILLED WITH THE ODOUR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and breathe slowly. Think of someone who deserves more praise than they get. A parent, a teacher, a friend, a coworker who quietly holds things together. Now, in your head, compose one extravagant compliment for them. Not a polite one. Too much. The kind that fills the room. Say exactly what they mean to you and why. Notice if it feels embarrassing. Mary's gift drew an objection at the table, and she gave it anyway. If you pray, you can give thanks for them. The bell holds the time.

Spikenard. The costly perfumed oil Mary poured, a whole pound of it, on Jesus's feet, and wiped with her own hair. This week's words: the keys, transfiguration, Zacchaeus up a sycamore, Lazarus, hosanna, the moneychangers' tables go over. And now three hundred pence poured out.
Your line: love can be lavish. Today, give that extravagant compliment, out loud or in writing, to the person you thought of. Day sixty-three.
